dialect is refused whole (`marketplace_catalog_other_dialect`), rather than
read by its place alone, which would refuse every entry of it, or by its
shape alone, which would read a file neither agent reads as a catalog. One
whose entries say both, or neither, an empty one among them, is read as its
place says, each entry of the other's shape failing on its own. No column
keeps the dialect: a gather again reads the catalog again, and finds it as
it is then. A Codex entry is its name and a `local` source,
`{"source": "local", "path": "./x"}`, whose path starts `./` and names a
folder below the marketplace's, as Codex resolves one (`Plugin::Local`,
listed as `local`); what else it holds, the `policy` and the `category`
Codex requires and any key only Claude Code's format gives, is read past,
and one Codex would not resolve, a source of another kind, a path not
starting `./`, or one naming the marketplace's folder itself, is skipped
with a failure of its own (`marketplace_entry_unresolved`), as Codex skips
it, the rest listed and gathered as a Claude Code catalog's are, `--list`,
`--plugin` and `--all` alike. One climbing out is refused as a relative
entry is (`marketplace_entry_outside`), and one whose folder is not there
or leads out through a link is held to the clone as a relative one is.

Where a plugin is (`marketplace::Plugin`) is held as a folder of a
repository is. A relative one, `./x`, `.` or a bare name read under the
catalog's `metadata.pluginRoot`, is a folder of the marketplace's own
repository, refused when it is absolute or climbs out lexically, and once
the catalog is read from its clone when it is not there or leads out of it
through a link (`marketplace_entry_outside`, `marketplace_entry_missing`),
as `--path` is held. A `github` one names `owner/repo` and nothing else, so
it is GitHub's; a `url` or `git-subdir` one names a repository on another
machine (`url::is_remote`), a `git-subdir`'s path held to its repository
lexically. One naming a folder on this machine is refused
(`marketplace_entry_local`): a catalog is somebody else's file, and one
naming any folder of the disk would have a gather put whatever it held on
the shelf, which no plugin in the marketplace's own repository can, held as
it is to that repository.

The marketplace is a source of the kind `marketplace`, so a repository
gathered whole and the same repository listed as a catalog are two
sources. It is registered, fetched into its folder of the cache, read and
recorded under the workspace's lock, as one source's gather is, and called
`--name`'s name, the name it has, or the catalog's own, held to
`SourceName::parse` (`marketplace_name_unusable`) and numbered when another
source has it, as a name a URL gives is, where a `--name` another has is
refused. One this registered is forgotten again, its clone with it, when its
catalog cannot be fetched or read, or the gather is cancelled: what it is
called is the catalog's to say, and a catalog never read says nothing, so a
source left registered would be called what no catalog named it. The log
says its fetch as a gather's.

Each plugin gathered is a git source of its own with the marketplace as
its parent and the name its catalog lists it by as its entry
(`LedgerStore::child_for`), found again by that entry whatever it is called
and moved to where the catalog says its plugin is now, its folder kept,
since the catalog is what says where a plugin is. It is called
`<marketplace>.<plugin>` (`SourceName::child`), with the marketplace's name
in it because two marketplaces list plugins of one name, and a numbered one
would say nothing of which. Its folder on the shelf and in the cache is the
marketplace's followed by its entry, each character a folder name does not
keep a hyphen, and never `.` or `..`: an entry is the catalog's text, and
read as a URL's folder is, `x@..` would keep what follows its `@` and be the
cache itself, which a fetch replaces whole. A source whose recorded folder
is no one folder name, which only a hand edit makes, is refused by a gather
before anything is fetched or placed (`source_folder_not_its_own`), as
`gather remove` refuses it. A plugin in the marketplace's own repository is
gathered from the marketplace's clone while the lock its catalog was read
under is still held, so nothing fetches into it between, and has no clone of
its own; one in a repository of its own is a gather of its own afterwards,
as `gather update` gathers a source after another, at the `ref` and the
`sha` its entry names, the `sha` held to a pin's rules and fetched as
`--pin` fetches one, the commit it took being the pin (`gather::refused`,
`gather::fetch`). Each is searched as a plugin (`gather::Search::Plugin`):
the skills its entry names, each a folder from the plugin's root held to the
repository lexically (`gathered_listed_outside`), through links, as every
candidate is, and to holding a `SKILL.md` (`gathered_listed_missing`), as
anthropics/skills names its two plugins' skills; and with none named, its
`skills/` folder and the folders its manifest names, each searched as a
repository is, or a `SKILL.md` at its root.

A plugin's own manifest (`plugin::Manifest`, #104) is read from
`.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, a `plugin.json` at its root whose `$schema`
names the Agent Plugins format, or `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, the format
of the agent its catalog is for looked for first
(`plugin::Format::read_for`): Codex's catalog's plugin is read as Codex
reads it. It is JSON somebody else wrote, read as a catalog is, as JSON
alone, to `plugin::MANIFEST_CAP`, never through a link out of its clone. A
Codex or a Claude Code one, whose place says what it is, that cannot be
read is said (`gathered_manifest_unreadable`) and the plugin searched as if
it had none, since one broken file is no reason not to take the skills
beside it; a root `plugin.json` that does not say it is the Agent Plugins
format's, or cannot be read as one, is anybody's file and passed over. What
it names under `skills` is searched beside `skills/`, for both agents'
manifests, each held to the repository lexically
(`gathered_manifest_outside`): taking one and not the other on an agent's
behalf would guess at what that agent loads, where taking both leaves
nothing a plugin offers off the shelf. A package in the Agent Plugins
format offers its `skills/<child>` alone (`gather::candidates`), never
deeper and no `SKILL.md` at its root, as that format says, so it is not
searched to `SEARCH_DEPTH`: the folder a gather searches, a plugin a
catalog lists or a repository `gather git` gathers, and any folder a
repository's search comes to that is one (`plugin::is_package`). What a
catalog's entry names is still the plugin's skills, as the catalog says
them. A repository gathered whole is searched as #101 searched it whatever
agent's manifest it holds, since a manifest says how an agent reads a
plugin, and a repository is no plugin until a catalog lists it.

A plugin's licence, as its manifest gives it and then as the catalog does,
is a skill's that says none
([what each artifact is recorded with](#what-each-artifact-is-recorded-with)).
What a plugin holds beside its skills, its hooks, its agents and its MCP
servers, as its entry or its manifest declares them or its folder keeps
them (`marketplace::Holding`), is said in a note and never taken: none of
it is a skill, and each is something an agent runs. A manifest declares one
by a path only while something is at that path in the plugin, and by a list
of paths, as Claude Code's lists its agents' and hooks' files, only while
something is at one of them, since a path that keeps nothing holds nothing
to say. Its MCP servers are kept in
`.mcp.json` or in `mcp.json` (`marketplace::MCP_FILES`, #104), and the note
names the file each is in (`Child::mcp_files`), so a person knows which to
read; nothing of either is imported, which this roadmap never does. A
package in the Agent Plugins format that `gather git` gathers, the folder
it searches, is said the same way (`gather::Report::holds`), since it is a
plugin by its own `plugin.json` with no catalog to list it; one a
repository's search comes to below that folder is not (open questions). A
plugin that is one skill, its `SKILL.md` at its root or its root the skill
its entry names, is put on the shelf without them, where it keeps each
(`hooks`, `agents`, `.mcp.json`, `mcp.json`), as a skill's
`.claude-plugin` is left off, and compared without them too. Each
plugin's gather is watched, cancelled before it places and logged as a
gather is; one that fails is said by its entry beside the rest, and once one
is cancelled the rest are not begun.

The schema's ninth step is what keeps them ([why the ledger is
SQLite](#why-the-ledger-is-sqlite)): `entry` beside the `parent_id` version 7
gave `sources` for it, one source an entry of its marketplace
(`sources_by_entry`), and the identity a gather finds a source by held among
the sources gathered on their own, since a plugin is no longer the
repository it is in: anthropics/skills lists two plugins, each the whole of
its repository. A plugin's branch is kept in `reference_key` alone, since
version 1's `UNIQUE (kind, url, reference, subdirectory)`, which no `ALTER`
drops, finds no row equal to one whose `reference` is `NULL`.

A marketplace's own commands cascade. `gather update` of it fetches its
catalog again and gathers every plugin of it gathered before from where the
catalog says it is now (`marketplace::again`, `Pick::Recorded`), saying one
it lists no more (`marketplace_entry_unlisted`) and keeping its source as it
was, for `gather remove` to take away; of one plugin, it gathers that plugin
alone through its marketplace's catalog, which is what says where it is and
at which commit, and of a plugin and its marketplace, the marketplace's;
`--all` gathers each marketplace once with its plugins (`sources::Again`).
`gather remove` of it says, then takes, each plugin of it, its folders and
rows, before its own clone and row, so a folder that will not go keeps every
row of a source that still holds one. `gather sources` lists each plugin
right after its marketplace, its name indented, and the marketplace by how
many plugins of it are gathered; `--json` gives each source's `parent`, by
its name, and `entry`.

`gather marketplace` is the network, `--list` too, which fetches the
catalog, and it says each step and honours a cancel as `gather git` does,
through the watch the catalog's request and each plugin's carry: so a
front end with no terminal runs it as it runs `gather git`, the panel's
server telling each step and taking the cancel ([progress and
cancel](#progress-and-cancel)). The TUI's shelf page lists a marketplace's
plugins with `m` and gathers the ticked ones ([a gather runs
apart](#a-gather-runs-apart)).

### What each artifact is recorded with

Each artifact the shelf holds is recorded with where it came from, to the
commit (#99): its `revision`, the commit it was taken at, as it has been
since schema 1; its `upstream_path`, its folder in the repository from the
repository's root, `/` separated, by its lexical route from the clone's
root, so a folder typed `./skills/` is `skills`; the `content_hash` of the
copy on the shelf, by `hash::tree`, the recipe an install keeps of a copy,
so a copy installed from it hashes alike, the shelf holding no top-level
`.claude-plugin` since #101, as no installed copy does, and taken of the shelf rather
than the clone, since a link in the clone is what the copy resolved and the
hash refuses a link; and its `license`, as written. One that cannot be read
back to be hashed is recorded with no hash and said with a failure of its
own (`gathered_unhashed`), as an install records a copy it cannot read
back, rather than not at all. A rule's `upstream_path` is its file, and its
hash `hash::bytes` of it, a rule's install's recipe, and its licence is
read as [gathering rules](#gathering-rules) says.

The licence is the skill's `license`, as its manifest states it, whatever
it says (a name, an SPDX expression, `Complete terms in LICENSE.txt`); else
what a licence file beside the manifest names, `LICENSE` or `LICENCE`,
bare, as Markdown or as text, in any case, the bare one first; else, for a
skill of a plugin a marketplace lists or of an Agent Plugins package, the
folder gathered or one its search comes to, the plugin's licence as its own
manifest gives it (#104), the package's nearest the skill first, then as
its catalog gives it (#103), what the skill says of itself being nearer to
it than what its plugin says, and what a plugin says of itself nearer than
what a catalog says of the plugin it lists; else none, which is unknown, and
`gather list` says so. Of a file, the identifier a
line of it tags with `SPDX-License-Identifier:`, since that is the licence
named in the one spelling every tool reads, put there to be found; and
otherwise its first line that is not blank, which is how a licence's text
opens (`MIT License`, `Apache License`), its title as the file writes it.
The first line alone was the other way, and loses what a tag says
exactly; the tag alone, the other, and finds nothing in most files, which
carry none. Telling a licence from the whole of its text, as GitHub's
licensee does, would be a guess recorded as a fact: what is recorded is
what the skill says, and reading the text is left to whoever reads it. A
title names no version (`Apache License` is followed by `Version 2.0` on
the next line), which a tag does. The file is read from the shelf, the head
of it alone, so a licence file that is a link is read as the copy resolved
it, within the clone, never followed anywhere else, and one that cannot be
read names nothing, as one that is not there: the hash, which reads every
file of the copy, has said already that one cannot be. A repository's own
licence, at its root or as a forge's API says it, is not the skill's
folder's and is not read, unless the skill is the whole repository, whose
root is its folder.

### Following a gather, and stopping it

A gather is the network, so it can take long enough that somebody wants to
know how it is going, and to change their mind. A `gather::Request` carries a
`Watch`: a callback the gather tells each `Progress` to, and a flag that
cancels it. Both are core's own types. `gix` has a progress tree and an
interrupt flag of its own, and handing those to the front ends would tie each
of them, the server that streams progress ([progress and
cancel](#progress-and-cancel)) included, to gix's version and to the names
it gives its steps.

The steps are connecting, receiving objects, resolving deltas, checking out
files, reading the folders that hold a manifest, `n` of `m`, and placing what
was read on the shelf, `n` of `m`. The counts during the fetch are gix's: the
clone hands it a progress tree and reads it from a thread of its own ten times
a second, because gix counts most of its work on shared atomics, from threads
of its own, without telling the progress anything. The counts are picked out
by the identifiers gix gives them, not the names it shows, which it is free to
reword. That thread is joined before the clone says its next step, so a front
end never hears a count after the step that follows it. The callback is a
plain `Fn` that is `Send` and `Sync`, rather than a channel, so each front end
chooses how the news travels: the CLI writes a line, the TUI sends it to the
thread that draws, and a server can stream it.

The flag is gix's interrupt, so a cancel stops the fetch or the checkout where
gix checks, and the clone it had begun is removed. gix does not check it while
it connects, only once the pack is coming, so a cancel while connecting waits
for the connection to be made or to fail: as long as a server takes to answer,
or a prompt to be answered. One made while the gather waits for [the
workspace's lock](#writers-at-the-same-time) waits too, since nothing checks
the flag until the lock is held: as long as the writer holding it takes, and a
wait that runs out ends the gather as busy rather than cancelled, unlogged all
the same. The harvest checks it once more after every folder
is read and before anything is placed, which is why it reads them all first
rather than reading and placing each in turn. That is the last moment a cancel
is honoured: past it the shelf and the ledger change, and a gather stopped
halfway through that would leave them neither as they were nor as the source
has them. A cancel that comes later is too late, and the gather finishes.
`Progress::cancellable` says which steps are which, so a front end that offers
a cancel stops offering it when the gather stops honouring it, rather than
knowing where the check is. Cancelled in time, the shelf and the ledger are as
they were: the gather is not logged, and a source it registered is forgotten
again, and a source a `--name` renamed is called what it was. It is
registered before the fetch because the clone needs the folder
name registering gives it; holding the registration in a transaction until the
gather ends was the other way, and is rejected, because every other write to
the ledger would wait as long as the network does. The clone is not part of the
promise: every gather re-makes it, so a cancelled one can leave a known source
with the new clone, or with none.

`mindweaver gather` on a terminal draws each step over the last on one line of
stderr, and wipes it before the report. Piped or captured it draws nothing,
so what it prints there is what it always printed. The binaries run every
line with that line's watch (`run_watched`, `run_weaver_cli_watched`), and
`run` and `run_weaver_cli`, which the tests call, with one nobody follows. The
TUI runs a gather on a thread of its own, and `esc` cancels it ([A gather runs
apart](#a-gather-runs-apart)); the panel's server tells each step on its
stream, and `POST /api/v1/commands/cancel` cancels it ([progress and
cancel](#progress-and-cancel)).

### Why `gix` rather than running `git`

Nothing depends on a `git` being installed, or on which `git` is first on the
PATH, and core keeps doing its own I/O rather than supervising a process. The
cost is that authentication for private repositories is ours to solve rather
than inherited whole from `git`.

Half of it is solved: a fetch **never prompts** for a credential. When a server
asks who is fetching, `gix`'s own answer runs the credential helpers git config
names and, when none of them has a credential, asks a person: an askpass
program, then the terminal. The TUI owns the terminal while a gather runs, so
that prompt is drawn over, its keys raced for, and the server that comes next
has no terminal at all. So every connection `gix` lets a clone configure is
given a credentials callback (`gather::credentials`) that runs the same helper
cascade with the prompt and askpass turned off. A credential no helper has is
`GitError::Credentials`: the URL without its credentials, and the two ways to
provide one, a git credential helper or, for an ssh URL, ssh-agent. Over ssh,
`gix` runs the system `ssh`, which authenticates with keys of its own and asks
the helpers only for a user name, so a login ssh refuses is reported the same
way. Whether a fetch went over ssh is read from the URL `gix` connected to, not
the one typed: git config's `url.<base>.insteadOf` can turn a typed https URL
into an ssh one, or the reverse. What ssh itself asks on the terminal is
outside the callback's reach, and so is the one connection `gix` opens without
letting the clone configure it; both are [open questions](#open-questions).

The callback is set on the connection rather than asked for through git
config (`gitoxide.credentials.terminalPrompt=false`), which would also stop
the prompt: the guarantee then lives in code a test reaches, not in a string
among the user's own settings, and the credential a front end supplies needs
the callback to arrive through anyway. That other half is
[D-16](#d-16-credentials-come-from-the-front-end-never-from-a-prompt)'s.

`gix`'s error types are large and would become part of this crate's public API
if they were carried, tying its version to gix's, so `GitError` keeps what they
said and not what they were.

### A URL is kept without its credentials

A source is stored, logged, listed and named in errors by its URL, so a token
typed into one would be repeated everywhere: in `mindweaver.db`, in the
clone's `.git/config`, in every report, in the snapshot every front end reads
([the read model](#the-read-model)), in `--json` output and soon in the
panel. One function takes it out, `url::redacted`, and
everything that keeps or shows a URL goes through it.

What it takes out is everything before the `@` of a `scheme://` URL, except
the user name of an ssh URL: that is who ssh logs in as, part of where the
repository is rather than a secret, and a later gather from the stored URL
needs it. Over http(s) a user name goes as well, because GitHub takes a token
in that place and a credential helper is what names the user. The scp-like
form (`git@host:path`) is left alone, since `gix` reads everything before its
first `:` as user and host, which leaves no room for a password. A password
with a `/` in it is looked for past the first `/`, whenever what comes before
that `/` has a `:` and no port: every parser reads `https://me:p/ss@host` as
host `me` and port `p`, so nothing else would find the password, and the
refusal for an unparseable URL would store and print it whole. It works on
text rather than on one URL, because the other place a credential turns up is
`gix`'s own error messages, which quote the URL they failed on, and the URL a
fetch connected to may carry a token the typed one did not when git config
rewrites it with `url.<base>.insteadOf`. Parsing with `gix::url` and dropping
the user was rejected: the parser also rewrites what it keeps, a default port
dropped or a scheme lowercased, and cannot find a URL inside a sentence.

A gather URL that carries a credential is **refused** before anything is
registered or fetched, rather than used for that one fetch and stored without
it: a token on the command line is already where `ps` and the shell history
show it, and refusing is what points at a git credential helper, which keeps
it off the command line altogether, as the front-end provider of
[D-16](#d-16-credentials-come-from-the-front-end-never-from-a-prompt) will.
So is such a URL typed where the branch or the folder goes: the ledger keeps
a source's branch and folder word for word, since neither is a URL, and a
`GitError` would quote the branch, so a token typed there, found by the
suite that tries every credentialed form in every place a gather takes text,
was stored and printed until it was refused alike, and so is one typed as
the name (`--name`), which a name could never hold anyway. Behind that refusal the rest holds whichever caller is writing. The ledger
redacts every URL on the way in and again on the way out, so nothing it hands
back carries a credential, scrubbed yet or not. Every `GitError` redacts the
URL and what `gix` said. A clone is scrubbed as soon as it is made (the gix
adapter's `Remote::scrub`, [values, ports and
adapters](#values-ports-and-adapters)): `gix` writes the URL into the remote's entry in `.git/config`
and into every reflog as `clone: from <url>`, and those files are rewritten
through the same function. A clone a gather makes now has nothing to take out,
and finding that costs a few small reads. A `--from` typed with credentials
names the source they were taken out of. The CLI's report prints URLs
redacted, and a task's command line is redacted where it is built for
showing (`task::shell`), so the box that says what is running and the
transcript printed on the way out both leave the token out.

What a Mindweaver from before the refusal stored is **scrubbed** when a
command that writes opens the ledger. `WeaverWorkspace::ledger_to_write` is
the one way to open it for writing: it runs `gather::scrub`, which only core
can call, and hands back what that took out for the front end to say, the way
`resolve` with `Intent::Write` is the one way to find a workspace that may be
created. Which commands write is the front end's to know, but what opening to
write involves is core's, so no front end can write first and scrub after.
`gather git`, `install` and `uninstall` open it that way, as do
`install::disown` and `install::carry`, through which core's lifecycle changes
(`lifecycle::add`, `rename` and `remove`) drop or carry a record. Each hands
back what the scrub took out (its result's `scrub`) beside what it did to the
record, since a scrub says what it found only the first time and a change that
dropped it would leave it unsaid for good. `rename` opens the ledger once for
each name and tells what both scrubs found once (`Scrub::absorb`): the second
finds only the clones the first could not rewrite. So does the install screen,
in both screens, when what it marked is applied rather than as it opens,
which is a read ([A read leaves the ledger as it finds
it](#a-read-leaves-the-ledger-as-it-finds-it)): applying runs the `install`
and `uninstall` lines its marks amount to, and the first of them opens the
ledger to write, scrubbing it, as from the shell. A scrub made two sources one
row before schema 7, when a mark on the row that went would have installed
from folders the scrub removed; since that step, two rows only a credential
told apart are one source already, made one as the ledger was opened, the
screen's reading included, so no scrub drops a row a mark is on. Scrubbing as
the screen opened is still rejected: opening it is a read. An edit writes
nothing to the ledger, since it keeps the record as it was, so `finish_edit`
only reads it (`ledger_for_reading`) and scrubs nothing.

The scrub rewrites the sources whose URL carries a credential, each clone made
from one, the origin of every installation from one, which schema 3 copied
from the URL as it was stored, and the action log. A clone is rewritten before
its row, so a clone that cannot be rewritten keeps its row tainted and is
tried again next time, as a warning; what was taken out is a note, said once,
since the command did what it was asked and an exit code that failed because
of a fix would break a script for nothing it did. Two rows whose URLs only a
credential told apart, with the same branch and folder, are one place
gathered twice, which the step to schema 7 makes one row, as it does two
spellings of one URL ([why the ledger is SQLite](#why-the-ledger-is-sqlite)),
before the scrub ever sees them: the URL a source is known by holds no
credential. Before that step the scrub made them one itself, by the rule the
step keeps: the row kept is the one whose shelf was filled most recently,
since its folder holds the newer files, and a row whose gather failed before
it took anything loses however recently it was tried. What the other row
gathered goes with it, and its clone and shelf folder are removed (a folder
that will not go is a warning), rather than its records moving to the kept
row: they would point into a folder the ledger no longer reserves, which the
next source with the same readable name would be given and gather over. The
ledger turns on SQLite's `secure_delete`, so a rewritten row leaves no copy of
its old text in the file's free space.

It runs every time rather than once, as a schema step would, because an older
build could keep writing to the same file after a newer one had scrubbed it,
and the schema steps are spoken for by the changes that need a new version.
Schema 3 is a file such a build refuses, so the scrub could now be part of
that step, and schema 7, which makes rows one, could have been; whether it
should is open (see the open questions). Schema 7 runs it again only in that
the first command that writes after the step scrubs what the step left,
the clones of the rows it kept among it. With
nothing to do it still reads, every time a command writes: a scan of the
sources and one of the action log, in a transaction. Neither can use an index,
so the log's grows with the log, and every entry naming an ssh URL, which
keeps its `@`, is read and found clean again each time. Recording that the log
had been scrubbed would skip that, and is rejected for the reason the scrub
runs every time: an older build writing a token again would go unnoticed. The
cost ends when the scrub can stop (see the open questions). A read is left
alone: what it shows is redacted on the way out anyway, and a read should not
write. Until a command that writes scrubs it, a place an older build gathered
both with a token and without one is read as the file has it, two sources
offering each skill under one origin. Deleting the old
clones instead of rewriting them would have been simpler and was rejected:
the clone is kept so a gather can be looked at afterwards, and a scrub has no
reason to take that away.

### Why the ledger is SQLite

Everything else Mindweaver writes is a file a person opens: TOML with comments
explaining itself. `mindweaver.db` is not, and the exception is deliberate. It
answers questions a file cannot (which of two identically named skills came
from which repository, at which revision, and what happened the last four times
a gather ran), and answering them from a flat file would mean writing a query
engine badly.

It sits in `.mindweaver/`, beside the marker it belongs to, so it travels with
the workspace and two workspaces never share a history. It carries its schema
version in SQLite's own `user_version` header field, and a database from the
future is refused exactly as a marker file from the future is. The first
command that writes to it makes it; a read never does, and changes an existing
one only to migrate it ([A read leaves the ledger as it finds
it](#a-read-leaves-the-ledger-as-it-finds-it)).

Six things are recorded: the **sources** gathered from, each by its name and
the identity of its URL ([everything is namespaced by its
source](#everything-is-namespaced-by-its-source)), the **artifacts** on
the shelf and which source each came from, the **installations** (which skill,
rule or MCP server Mindweaver put into which project, from where, every copy it
wrote and a hash of what it wrote, or for a server every entry it wrote into
an agent's config file and the fingerprint of each), the **files Mindweaver
made** in a project, which it
may take away again, the **projects** by the id each was last seen holding,
and an **action log**. The log keeps failures too: a log
of only what worked cannot answer the question anybody opens it with.
Timestamps are Unix seconds, which needs no date library and which SQLite
renders with `datetime(at, 'unixepoch')`.

No URL this build writes into it, or reads back out of it, carries a
credential. One an older build stored stays in the file until the next command
that writes scrubs it, and for good in the copy a schema step took before that
(see the open questions). An older build could store one again after a scrub
until schema 3, which it refuses
([A URL is kept without its credentials](#a-url-is-kept-without-its-credentials)).

A source's shelf folder is stored rather than derived: two URLs can reduce to
the same readable name, and where a source's files went is a fact about the
past that must not move when the naming rule changes.

The schema has had ten versions, each a block in the SQLite store's
migration (`adapter::sqlite::Sqlite::migrate`) and a
constant beside it:

1. `sources`, `artifacts` and `actions`: what was gathered, from where, and
   what happened.
2. `installations`: which artifact went into which project, which is what
   lets an uninstall tell Mindweaver's copy from somebody's.
3. `installation_targets`, one row for each copy an installation wrote, with
   the agent it is for when it is one agent's
   ([D-07](#d-07-one-copy-per-agent-folder)); and on `installations`, the
   `origin` it came from, spelled as `--from` takes it, and the
   `content_hash` of what it wrote
   ([D-04](#d-04-an-edited-copy-is-detected-not-disowned)). The
   installation's own path moved into its one target, so a copy's path is
   kept in one place (#30).
4. A `content_hash` of each target's own, for a kind whose copies hold
   different bytes: a rule's section of the block in `AGENTS.md` and its
   file for Claude ([installing rules](#installing-rules)), each of which
   can be edited apart from the other. A skill's targets leave it empty,
   every one holding the tree the installation's hash names. And
   `created_files`, each file Mindweaver made in a project rather than
   wrote into, so the block goes with the last rule and the file with it
   only when Mindweaver made it (#45).
5. `projects`, the id the ledger last saw at each route, one id a route and
   one route an id, and on `installations`, the `project_id` each record was
   made for, so a project that moved is found again by its id ([an entry
   whose project moved](#an-entry-whose-project-moved), #57).
6. `installation_entries`, one row for each entry an MCP server's
   installation wrote into an agent's config file
   ([D-10](#d-10-an-mcp-server-is-one-owned-entry-per-agent)): the agent,
   the file as a route from the project, the server's name it is keyed by,
   and the `fingerprint` of what was written ([the
   fingerprint](#the-fingerprint)), one entry an agent (#93). A table of its
   own rather than more targets: a target is a copy found by its path, and
   an entry is found by its key in a file every server of the project
   shares. The definition's origin is the installation's `origin`, which
   version 3 added, so the step adds nothing for it.
7. On `sources`, a `name`, a `canonical_url` and a `reference_key`, empty
   for the remote's HEAD, unique behind `sources_by_name` and
   `sources_by_identity`, so a source is called by one name and is one
   repository however its URL is spelled (#98,
   [D-13](#d-13-sources-have-names-and-a-marketplace-is-a-parent), closing
   the hole #7 left); and `pin` and `parent_id`, for what a source is
   pinned to (#99) and the marketplace it is listed by (#103), which
   neither wrote at version 7. The columns go on the end of the table
   rather than into a new one, which would be copied in under foreign keys
   that cascade a dropped `sources` into every artifact, and the old
   `UNIQUE` stays, holding nothing the new index does not.
8. On `artifacts`, where each came from beyond the commit it was taken at,
   which `revision` has kept since version 1: its `upstream_path`, its
   folder in the repository, the `content_hash` of what the gather put on
   the shelf, by `hash::tree`, the one recipe installs use, and its
   `license` as the skill says it, empty when nothing does (#99). On the
   end of the table, as version 7 put a source's.
9. On `sources`, the `entry` a marketplace's catalog lists a plugin by,
   unique with its `parent_id` behind `sources_by_entry`, and
   `sources_by_identity` held among the sources gathered on their own, so a
   plugin is a source of its own wherever it is ([a marketplace and its
   plugins](#a-marketplace-and-its-plugins), #103). A plugin's branch is in
   `reference_key` alone, its `reference` left `NULL`, since version 1's
   `UNIQUE`, which no `ALTER` drops, would refuse two plugins of one
   repository at one branch, and finds no row equal to one whose `reference`
   is `NULL`; every read takes the branch from `reference_key` where
   `reference` holds none. Making the table again without it was the other
   way, and is rejected: the old table can be dropped only under foreign
   keys that cascade a dropped `sources` into every artifact, SQLite takes
   the switch that turns them off only outside a transaction, where every
   step runs, and renaming the old table away first follows it with every
   reference to it while they are on.
10. On `sources`, `gathers`, the kind of artifact a source's gather takes,
    `skill` or `rule`, held by `sources_by_identity` beside the rest, so
    one folder of one repository gathered for skills and for rules is two
    sources, each gathered again for what it took ([gathering
    rules](#gathering-rules), #111). A source of rules keeps its branch in
    `reference_key` alone, as a plugin does, for the reason version 9
    gives: version 1's `UNIQUE` would refuse it beside a source of skills
    from the same folder at the same branch, typed alike.

An older ledger is migrated step by step, so one made two versions ago ends
where one made today begins, and two rules hold for every step:

- **The file is copied aside first.** Before the first step, the ledger is
  copied beside itself as `mindweaver.db.v<old>.bak` (`Sqlite::back_up`), and
  nothing is migrated unless the copy is whole and opens at the old version.
  A step that turns out wrong then leaves the file it started from: the copy
  opens at the old version, and the build that wrote it reads it as it
  always did. It is named after the version it holds, so which build reads
  it is in its name, and a ledger brought forward by several builds in turn
  leaves one for each version it had. It is taken once the migration holds
  the write lock, not before: a copy taken after an unlocked read of the
  version could be of a ledger another process has since migrated, and would
  replace that process's copy of the old version with one of the new. It is
  SQLite's online backup rather than a copy of the file, because opening the
  file outside SQLite while a connection holds it would drop that
  connection's locks on Unix, and it reads through a second connection,
  because SQLite will not copy from one in the middle of writing. It goes
  through a temporary and a rename, so a copy cut short is never mistaken
  for a whole one, and the temporary is made with the ledger's permissions
  before anything is written to it, so a ledger kept private is not readable
  through its copy even while the copy is written. A step to come is one
  more block in `migrate`, and the copy is taken for it without its asking.
- **The steps run in one transaction**, with the stamp of the new version.
  Run a statement at a time, a step that failed, or a process that died
  halfway, left a database half migrated under its old version, which the
  next open would try to migrate again and fail on.

A step fills in what it can from what the version before recorded, spelled
as that version's code spelled it, in the step's own SQL rather than through
the code that spells it now: a later change to the spelling would otherwise
change what an earlier step wrote. Version 3 gives an installation from a
source that source's origin, and one from the workspace or a load none, since
version 2 kept nothing to say which; it makes up no hash for a copy nobody
hashed when it was written, and D-04 says how a missing one reads. Version 4
fills in nothing: no build before it installed a rule, and a skill's targets
need no hash of their own. Version 5 fills in what no SQL could: the file
kept no id, so the step is handed the id of each project the workspace
links, opened for its settings, with the route its records are under
(`Ledger::open_knowing`), and its own SQL writes them in. The one exception
to what a step is filled from, and the reason for it holds: what it is handed
is what the projects hold, not how today's code spells something. A project
a `mind.toml` marks, an entry that will not open and an id two linked
directories hold are handed in for none, and their records keep their route
alone. Version 6 fills in nothing: no build before it installed an MCP
server. Version 7 is handed, as values, what no SQL can work out of a
source's URL, as version 5 is handed each project's id: the identity it is
(`url::canonical`, the rule a gather finds a source by), the name a gather
would give it (`owner-repo`, `SourceName::derived`) and the URL without a
credential (`url::redacted`), each worked out before the step
(`spelled_sources`). Its own SQL writes each row's identity in, names each
source by what it is handed in the order the sources were first gathered,
the later of two that would take one name numbered, and makes rows that turn
out to be one place one, before the identity is made unique: the one whose shelf
was filled most recently is kept, by the rule the scrub keeps, what the
other gathered goes with it, and every installation from it is from the kept
one, its origin rewritten to the kept one's as version 3 spelled an origin,
without the credential the kept one's URL may still hold, so an update finds
where it came from offered there and no row is given one it did not hold. It
is the second
exception, and of another kind: what it is handed is what today's rules say
of each row, since no SQL can tell that two URLs are one repository's, and
once written into the row it is what a gather finds its source by. A build
that changes a rule changes which URLs are one, and so takes a step of its
own to write each identity again. Each row that went is kept in a table of
the step's own, `merged_sources`, by the URL it was gathered from without a
credential, its branch, its folder name and the source it is one with
(`LedgerStore::merged`), until the first command that writes has said it and
removed its clone and shelf folders, which nothing points into any more
(`gather::scrub`, holding the workspace while it does). Kept in the file
rather than handed back by the opening that took the step, because that is a
read as often as not, a `status` or a `list` after an upgrade, which says
nothing of the step and removes no folder: whichever command took it, the
first that writes says each merge, as it says what the scrub took out, and
says it again with each folder that will not go, which every command that
writes tries again, until it goes. While a merge is kept its folder name is
given to no new source, so no gather can clone into a folder about to be
removed. A credential is left where the scrub finds it, which rewrites a
clone before its row, and which the first command that writes runs next.
Version 8 fills in an artifact's place upstream in its own SQL, from what
version 1 already kept: its source's folder by its lexical route, as a
gather takes it, walked a folder at a time so `./skills/` and `skills//`
are `skills`, a `..` takes off the folder before it and the repository's
root (`.`) is nothing, joined by `/` to the folder it has on the shelf,
which keeps the name the source gave it ([the folder a skill lands
in](#everything-is-namespaced-by-its-source)). It makes
up no hash and no licence. Both could be read from the shelf as it is now,
but the shelf is a folder anybody can change, and a hash taken of it at the
step would vouch for bytes no gather placed: the next gather of its source
fills them in, as an install fills in a missing hash. Version 9 fills in
nothing: no build before it gathered a marketplace, so every row is a
source gathered on its own, the entry of none. Version 10 fills in nothing
but by the column's default: no build before it gathered anything but
skills.
D-04's states (#47) took no step of their own: what tells them apart is the hash each copy was written with, which versions
3 and 4 keep, and what the place it came from offers now, which is read where
it is offered rather than kept. A record with no hash is held to its offer
by the code that reads it (`install::standings`), since a step has no offer
to fill one in from, and the first install over it stores its hash. Each step
comes with a fixture of what the version before it wrote
(`apps/core/tests/fixtures/ledger-v<N>.sql`, dumped from a ledger that build
made), from which a test migrates, checks every row is kept, and opens the
copy at the old version.

The hash is `hash::tree`, its only definition: SHA-256 over every folder and
file under a copy, by their `/`-separated paths in byte order, each file's
length before its bytes. The order is not the filesystem's and the separator
not the platform's, so one tree hashes alike on Linux, macOS and Windows, and
alike in every agent's folder, since the copy's own folder is not part of it.
Folders count, so two copies hash alike exactly when `copy::same` calls them
the same. A link is refused rather than followed: Mindweaver never writes one
into a copy, since `copy::tree` copies what a link points at, and following
one could read anything. For a skill it is kept once per installation, not
once per target: every target is written from one copy, so one hash is what
each is compared with, and a copy somebody edited is the one whose own hash no
longer matches it. A rule's targets each keep their own, `hash::bytes` of
what each holds, since its section and its file are not the same bytes. An install records the hash of the copy as it stands once
written; one that cannot be read back is recorded with none rather than not
at all, since without a record it would be Foreign for good. That is a
`warning:` and a non-zero exit, and the log's entry says why, rather than a
plain success: a record with no hash is read as one from before hashes were
kept. No install leaves a copy it can tell holds what the hash refuses. A
link where no install writes one is an edit, which an install that is not
forced refuses and a forced one writes over, even when it points at the
same bytes, which `copy::same` follows it to (`Stage::place_over`): left as
it was, the copy would be recorded with no hash and read as edited still.
What is left is a copy changed between landing and being read back.

## Fetching over HTTP

Catalogs, the MCP Registry and the skill directories, are HTTP APIs, and
core reads them itself ([D-14](#d-14-core-owns-http-behind-a-seam)). What
is done with an answer is rules, and they are `http`'s; what carries the
bytes is the `Http` port, one request a call, its answer handed back as
soon as its status and headers are in. A transport carries bytes and
nothing more, so a fake in a test is held to every rule the network is:
`http::Client` follows the redirects, reads the body and holds it to its
limits, whichever transport brought it. The default transport is
`adapter::reqwest::Reqwest`, the reqwest gix's HTTP transport already
builds, with rustls, so a catalog adds no crate and no second TLS. It is
handed to the client as a parameter, never found in a global or the
environment. The MCP Registry is the first catalog read through it (#106,
[the MCP Registry](#the-mcp-registry)), and the skill directories the
second (#108, [the skill directories](#the-skill-directories)).

Everything blocks, as the rest of core does. A blocking client fits a
synchronous core, and the server already runs what its backend does on
tokio's blocking pool. An async client would have put a runtime into every
caller to save threads a command line never runs short of.

### Every answer held to a time and a size

A fetch has a **total** time, 30 seconds unless a caller says otherwise
(`http::Limits`), from sending the request to the body's last byte, every
redirect included, and connecting has ten of its own
(`adapter::reqwest::CONNECT_TIMEOUT`). One span for the exchange rather
than a timeout per read, which is what reqwest's client-wide timeout is in
its blocking client: a server sending one byte just before each read would
time out never trips one per read, and what somebody waiting on a command
feels is how long it takes. The adapter gives reqwest the time that is left
as the request's own timeout, which runs to the body's end, and the client
looks at the time after every read too, so a transport that ignores it
overruns it by one read and no more.

A body is held to **16 MiB** unless a caller says otherwise, counted as it
is read: a `Content-Length` over the cap is refused before a byte is read,
and below it the cap is still held to what arrives, since a length is only
what a server says, and a body with none says nothing. Nothing is
decompressed, since no feature that would is built, so the cap is on what
the client holds. A status that is not a success is a failure, since what a
404 or a 503 has in its body is not what was asked for.

Every request says who sends it, `mindweaver/<version>`, which GitHub's API
requires, and carries the headers its caller gave it and none of the
transport's choosing. Headers belong to the request: a credential a front
end supplies ([D-16](#d-16-credentials-come-from-the-front-end-never-from-a-prompt))
lasts one run, so it is handed in with each request that needs it rather
than kept on a client or a transport that would send it with the next.
`Request::credential` marks one, and `Authorization`, `Proxy-Authorization`
and `Cookie` are marked whoever adds them: a request is debugged without
them, reqwest is told they are sensitive, and an error names a header by
its name alone. The adapter reads no proxy from the environment, which core
never reads, so a proxy is a front end's to hand over, an [open
question](#open-questions).

### Which URL is fetched, and where a redirect may lead

A URL is fetched when it is https, or http to this machine (a loopback
address, or `localhost`), and carries no credential (`http::fetchable`).
Plain http elsewhere is refused: what a catalog lists is what gets
gathered, and soon commands an agent runs, and over plain http anybody on
the way can change it. This machine is where a test's server and a catalog
of one's own are, and the way there is nobody else's. A URL with a user, a
password or a token in it is refused rather than sent once and dropped from
what is shown, as a gather's is ([a URL is kept without its
credentials](#a-url-is-kept-without-its-credentials)): a credential goes
in a header, which is never shown.

Redirects are followed by the client, never by reqwest (`Policy::none`), so
a fake is held to the same rules: ten at most (`Limits::max_redirects`), a
loop among them, and each to a URL the same rule lets through, never to
another scheme or to plain http elsewhere. Leaving the origin is allowed,
since that is where a service keeps its downloads, but the request's
credentials stay behind: they were given for the server it named. reqwest
drops `Authorization` and `Cookie` on such a hop itself, and only those,
so a key in a header of a service's own naming would have gone along.

Every failure is an `HttpError`, each with a code of its own (`http_*`): a
timeout (`http_timed_out`), a body past the cap (`http_too_large`), a
connection not made (`http_connect_failed`), a status that is not a success
(`http_status_unsuccessful`), a rate limit (`http_rate_limited`), a redirect
refused or one too many, a body that is not the JSON a caller declared
(`http_json_invalid`). A rate limit is a `429`, or a `403` that says it is
one, no request left (`X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0`) or a wait asked for
(`Retry-After`), as GitHub's API answers each of its limits; a `403` that
says neither is a refusal like any other, a token without the right. When
it resets is said as the answer says it, from `Retry-After`, a wait in
seconds or a date, then `X-RateLimit-Reset`, seconds since the epoch, the
order GitHub asks a caller to read them in, and that the answer does not
say when it says neither (`http::Reset`). Said rather than waited out: a
command that slept for an hour on a front end's behalf would look hung. Every URL in
one, every word a transport or serde said among them, is a `Redacted`
([values, ports and adapters](#values-ports-and-adapters)): a transport's
words can quote the URL it failed on, and serde's a string of the body
where it wanted another type. A catalog's caller collects them as failures
beside what it read ([failures are collected, not
raised](#failures-are-collected-not-raised)).

### A listing a page at a time

An answer is read as the JSON its caller declares (`Fetched::json`), strict
JSON rather than the JSONC agents' config files are read as, and a listing
a page at a time (`Client::pages`): by the `Link` header's `rel="next"`, as
GitHub's API pages, by a number in a query parameter, one more each page,
until a page with nothing in it, or by a cursor each page carries in its
body (`Page::cursor`), as the MCP Registry pages, until a page carries none
or an empty one. A cursor is set as its parameter of the first page's URL,
in place of any the URL had, so the query the listing was asked with goes
with every page, and as a value, escaped: it is what a page said, and adds
no parameter of its own. Each next page is asked with the
first one's headers, its credentials only on the origin the first named,
as a redirect leaves them. A listing is read no further than the bound its
caller sets, so a cursor that never runs out ends: what was read is kept,
and the cut said beside it (`http_too_many_pages`). A page that cannot be
fetched or read fails the listing, since what came before it is a listing
cut short at a place nobody chose.

### Answers kept on disk

A client given a `Cache` keeps each `200` in the workspace's
`.mindweaver/cache/http` (`WeaverWorkspace::http_cache_dir`), serves it
again unasked while it is fresh, for as long as its caller says
(`Cache::fresh_for`, nothing by default), and otherwise asks the server
whether it changed, by the `ETag` or `Last-Modified` it came with: a `304`
is served from the cache and kept again from then. A request carrying a
credential goes past the cache both ways, since what a credential unlocked
is not left on disk for a request without one to read. An answer a
redirect brought from another URL is not kept either: an entry says
nothing of where its answer came from, and a relative `Link` in it is read
against that place, so a listing read again from the cache would follow it
from the URL asked, to pages the network never named. What the cache
serves came from the URL asked (`Fetched::url`). A workspace not made yet,
the default a read falls back to without making it, has no cache
(`Cache::of`): keeping an answer there would make its `.mindweaver` on a
read.

An entry is a file named for its URL's SHA-256: a URL with a query holds
`?`, `&`, `/` and `..` in any order and at any length, none of which may
reach a file name, and a digest is one plain name whatever the URL was.
The file holds a line of JSON saying its format, when it was kept and the
answer's `Content-Type`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified` and `Link`, then the body
as it came. Nothing of the request: not its headers, which are what a
credential travels in, and not its URL, but for what the answer says of it,
as it said it. A `Link` to a listing's next page repeats the URL's query,
as GitHub's does, and so can a body, and no rule of text tells a key there
from a page number, so a key goes in a header (`Request::credential`),
whose request goes past the cache, never in a query. No other header of
the answer is kept, `Set-Cookie` least of all.

It is written through a temporary file beside it and a rename, so a reader
finds an entry whole or not at all, and two writers of one entry leave the
last one whole; so it takes no lock. It is read leniently, as a cache can
be: an entry that cannot be read, or that another build wrote in a format
of its own, is a miss, said (`http_cache_unreadable`) and written over by
the answer fetched in its place, and one that cannot be kept is said
(`http_cache_unwritable`) beside the answer, which is still served. What
went wrong with the cache is said beside a fetch that fails too
(`http::Failed`), every page's before it for a listing: nothing writes
over an unreadable entry then, so it would go unsaid for as long as the
fetch kept failing.

`cache/http` sits beside the clones, each a folder of the cache named from
its source, so it is kept from ever being one: the ledger takes `http` as
a folder in use when it gives a source one (`LedgerStore::source_for`,
`child_for`), so a source whose URL reads as `http` is gathered into
`http-2`, as one whose folder another source has is. A source a build from
before recorded with it is not fetched into it (`gather::own_folder`, the
refusal a row edited by hand meets, `source_folder_not_its_own`), so no
clone replaces the cache's answers; `gather remove` takes it, and the
cache's answers with its folder, which are only kept answers, and its URL
gathered again is given a folder of its own. A folder outside the cache,
`.mindweaver/http`, was the other way: the cache is where a workspace keeps
what it may throw away and fetch again, which its own folders are already
refused to overlap ([the workspace's own
artifacts](#the-workspaces-own-artifacts)), and a folder beside the marker
would be one more for that refusal to learn.

### The MCP Registry

The official MCP Registry, `registry.modelcontextprotocol.io`, is the
first catalog read through the client (#106), by its `/v0.1` API, the one
the registry keeps stable while the rest of it is in preview
(`registry::Registry`, in `apps/core/src/registry.rs`). It is handed the
`Client` its caller made, so whether answers are kept is the caller's
(`Cache::of` the workspace's) and every page and every version fetched
goes through the client's limits and its cache; and where the registry is
is a parameter, the official one unless the caller names another
(`Registry::at`), so a test's fake, or a registry of somebody's own that
speaks the same API, is read the same way. Three reads, none of which
writes anything:

- **A search** (`Registry::search`): `servers?search=Q&version=latest`,
  the latest version of every server the registry matches, a hundred a
  page (`PAGE_SIZE`, the most it gives one) and paged by the cursor each
  page carries in its body ([a listing a page at a
  time](#a-listing-a-page-at-a-time)), to ten pages unless the caller says
  otherwise (`MAX_PAGES`), the cut said beside what was read.
- **One version** (`Registry::version`): `servers/NAME/versions/V`, `V`
  `latest` or a version as the registry names it, the server's name one
  segment of the path though it holds a `/`.
- **What changed since a time** (`Registry::updated_since`):
  `servers?updated_since=T`, every version and not only the latest, the
  deleted among them, each said `deleted`, so that what keeps a server
  the registry took away learns it rather than keeping it as it was. A
  refresh asks for this, rather than the whole registry again.

What it answers is JSON somebody else wrote, read leniently, as a
marketplace's catalog is ([a marketplace and its
plugins](#a-marketplace-and-its-plugins)): a page is read a server at a
time, so one that does not read, with no name, no version, or a key this
build reads given another shape, is said on its own
(`registry_server_unreadable`, by where it was listed) and the rest are
listed all the same; a key it does not know is passed over, so a later
schema reads as this one; and a name or a version that a list would show
as other than it is, a control character in it or a space at either end,
is no server's, since a front end would show a name the registry is then
asked for in vain. Every other string a front end is handed of it, a
title, a description, a time, a status word this build does not know, is
made printable first (`text::printable`, the function every row of the
CLI is made printable by, moved into core for it), and the registry's
address is kept as a `Redacted`. So is why a server did not read, which
quotes the string serde could not read, a URL with a credential in it as
likely as any, and whatever a manual step quotes of the registry. One
version asked for by name that does not read is the answer failing
(`http_json_invalid`), since there is no rest to list beside it.

What the registry says of a server of its own accord, under
`_meta["io.modelcontextprotocol.registry/official"]`, is read beside it:
its status (`registry::Status`: `active`, `deprecated`, `deleted`, or a
word this build does not know, kept as said), when it was published and
last changed, and whether it is the latest. A schema before 2025-09-29 put
the status in the server's own document, which is read when the metadata
says none. Each server read is stamped with when it was read
(`ServerVersion::fetched_at`, by a `Clock`), which what is imported says
it was fetched at. A listing serializes as the read type it is
(`ServerVersion`, `Listing`, and `Found` for one version, each name pinned
by a test), what it could not read and what went wrong as `code::Said`;
the `server.json` it was
read from is kept beside it, for the mapping, and serialized nowhere.

`mindweaver gather mcp search QUERY` (#107) prints a search, a row a
server by the name `gather mcp add` takes, its version, its status and its
description, `--json` the `Listing` in the envelope; a server that does not
read, a cut and the cache failing are each a warning with its code, which
fails it as a failure collected does. It is a read: the workspace is
resolved without being made, the default one in home included, and a
client keeps its answers only in the cache of one that is made
(`Cache::of`). The command builds the one transport, reqwest's
(`adapter::reqwest::Reqwest`), and hands it to core, reading no proxy,
since core's adapter reads none either (an [open
question](#open-questions)), and where the registry is is `--registry`'s,
the official one unless it names another, held to the client's rules
([which URL is fetched](#which-url-is-fetched-and-where-a-redirect-may-lead))
before anything is sent, so a test serves #106's fixtures on 127.0.0.1 in
its own process and names that. `gather mcp add SERVER` fetches one version
(`Registry::version`, `latest` unless `--version` names one) and says what
it maps to, as `show` lays a server out, then writes it into the library
with `--yes` ([an imported server, written into the
library](#an-imported-server-written-into-the-library)), and without it is
a read that writes and makes nothing. What the mapping left out is a
warning that fails nothing, since the definition is what was asked for;
the manual steps of a version nothing maps are warnings before the
refusal. Nothing the definition names is started: a test puts stand-ins
for `npx`, `uvx`, `docker` and `dnx` on the `PATH` of the built binary and
finds none run. A front end with no terminal runs neither
(`Refusal::Unwatched`): each waits on the registry's answer, within its
client's limit, saying no step and looking for no cancel, where a gather
says each step and stops on one ([progress and
cancel](#progress-and-cancel)); and neither with `--registry` whatever is
lifted later (`Refusal::Addressed`), which would have the server fetch
from an address a page picked.

A search made once can be read again from the answers the cache kept of
it, and from them alone (`registry::kept`): a client whose transport sends
nothing, told every entry is fresh, so a page the cache does not keep is
no listing at all rather than a fetch. It is how a front end that ran the
search as a command line reads what the line found, as the TUI does
([a registry search from the shelf](#a-registry-search-from-the-shelf)):
the line fetched, and the screen reads what it kept, rather than reading
the line's text back or asking the registry again on the thread that
draws. A workspace not made yet has no cache, so nothing is kept to read.

### The skill directories

`mindweaver gather search` asks the skill directories what they find for a
query (#108, [D-15](#d-15-skill-search-is-github-plus-opt-in-finders)), each
a **finder** (`finder::Finder`, in `apps/core/src/finder.rs`): GitHub's code
search, for a `SKILL.md` matching the query, its documented REST API; and
skills.sh's `/api/search` and api.claude-plugins.dev's
`/api/skills/search`, marked unstable (`Finder::is_unstable`), since
neither is documented and each is read as it answers today, from the shape
the clients that use them read, written into this repository's fixtures by
hand. A finder only helps find a skill: each result names a repository and
a folder in it, and what is taken of it is gathered from git, as `gather
git --path` gathers it, so a directory whose answers change, or that goes
away, breaks nothing on the shelf, and its failure is a warning. A finder
is never a source: nothing it says is recorded but what the gather that
takes it records.

**Off until listed.** A finder is asked only when the workspace's marker
lists it, `finders = ["github", "skills.sh", "claude-plugins.dev"]`, which
nothing but a person writes (`finder::enabled`), since two of them are
services whose terms the person reads first (D-15). `--finder` asks those it
names alone, each listed, one that is not refused before any is asked
(`finder_not_enabled`), and none listed is refused too
(`finder_none_enabled`). A name this build does not know is passed over and
said (`finder_unknown`), rather than refused, so a marker a later build
listed a finder of its own in still reads. The key moves no
`WEAVER_FORMAT_VERSION`, as `known` did not ([formats are
versioned](#formats-are-versioned)). Directories that need a key of their
own, SkillsMP, Glama and skills.sh's v1 API, are not finders (D-15).

**Through the client, a token only to GitHub.** Each finder is asked
through the `Client` its caller hands over (`finder::Search`), one page of
`PER_FINDER` results, twenty, at its own address unless the caller names
another that speaks its API (`Search::at`, `--finder-url`, a GitHub
Enterprise server's `/api/v3` among them, read by `finder::located`), so
whether answers are kept, and over which transport, is the caller's, and a
test's is a fake or a server on 127.0.0.1. GitHub's code search answers no
request without a token, so it is asked only with one, which a front end
supplies for one search as a `finder::Token`, a value with no `Display` and
no `Serialize`, whose `Debug` says only that it is one: the CLI reads it
from the variable `--token-env` names
([D-16](#d-16-credentials-come-from-the-front-end-never-from-a-prompt)'s
option, the one #110 gives `gather git`), since core never reads the
environment, and core sends it as a credential (`Request::credential`),
which goes to the origin the request named alone, past a redirect
elsewhere, and keeps the request out of the cache both ways ([answers kept
on disk](#answers-kept-on-disk)). Without one, GitHub is skipped, sent
nothing, and said with a hint that fails nothing (`Found::skipped`); a
variable named that is not set is a warning (`token_env_unset`). `gh auth
token` is #110's.

**What they answer is untrusted.** An answer is read a result at a time,
as a registry's is: one whose shape this build does not read, an
undocumented API that changed, is a failure of that finder alone
(`finder_answer_unreadable`) beside what the others found; one that cannot
be reached, is not JSON or is rate limited is the client's error, carried
(`http_rate_limited` saying when the limit resets, when the answer says).
A result is dropped and said (`finder_result_dropped`) unless it resolves
to a git source `gather git` would take: a repository it names, read by
`url::address` so a tree URL's branch and folder are its own, with no
credential in it, which is never repeated, a folder that does not climb out
of it (`gather::outside`), and none of them with a control character in
it. A repository on this machine, a path, is taken from a finder on this
machine alone (`http::on_this_machine`), one of a person's own or a test's:
a service elsewhere naming one would have a gather put on the shelf whatever
a folder here holds, as a marketplace's catalog may not. Every string a
front end is handed is made printable. A result two finders name is listed
once (`Found::add`), by its repository as `url::canonical` spells every
spelling of it and its folder, which holds one skill, with each finder that
found it and the counts each gave. One with no folder, as skills.sh gives
every result, is told by its name too: by its repository alone, every skill
such a finder lists of one repository would be folded into the first,
unsaid. The results come in `Finder::ALL`'s order, GitHub's
first, each finder's in the order it ranked them, which is what `--take N`
counts by (`Found::take`). What was found serializes as `finder::Found`,
its results each a `finder::Hit`, by name ([the read types
serialize](#the-read-types-serialize)).

`mindweaver gather search QUERY` prints a row a result, numbered, `--json`
the `Found` in the envelope; a failure, a dropped result and the cache
failing are each a warning with its code, which fails it as a failure
collected does. It is a read, resolved without making the workspace, its
answers kept only in the cache of one that is made, and builds the one
reqwest transport `gather mcp` builds. `--take N` gathers the result listed
`N` instead, a write that makes the workspace as a gather does, through the
gather's own request (`Request::addressed`) and `gather::gather`, saying
first the `gather git` line it amounts to, spelled by the task module
(`Task::Gather`), so it can be read, or run again, without searching. The
number is the result's as this search lists it, so a finder that answers
differently can move it; one it does not list is refused
(`search_result_missing`) before anything is written. A result with no
folder is gathered from the repository's root, as `gather git` with no
`--path` gathers it, every skill the repository holds with it: skills.sh
names a skill's repository and never its folder, so what it found is not
told from the rest there (an [open question](#open-questions)). A front end
with no terminal runs neither (`Refusal::Unwatched`), as it runs no search
of the registry, for the same reason; and never one with `--finder-url`
(`Refusal::Addressed`) or `--token-env` (`Refusal::Environment`), which
would have the server fetch from an address a page picked, or read its own
environment and send what it found there.

A search made once is read again from the answers the cache kept of it
(`finder::kept`), as a registry's is: the same finders, through a client
whose transport sends nothing, every entry kept since the search started
fresh, and none kept before (`Cache::kept_since`). The command's client
asks every finder, nothing served unasked, and keeps each answer it is
given, or that it is told has not changed, from then; a finder that fails
it, rate limited or down, leaves the answer an earlier search kept, which
this search did not list, and reading that one again would list results
beside the warning that the finder failed, numbered otherwise than the
line numbered them. It is told by the second an entry is stamped with, so
a search made twice within one second is the one case it cannot tell
apart. GitHub's answers to a token were never kept, so a search read again
skips GitHub, and a finder whose answer the cache does not keep from then
is left out; one keeping none is no listing at all. It is how the TUI reads
what its search line found ([a skill search from the
shelf](#a-skill-search-from-the-shelf)), from when it started the line
(`Running::started`).

## Installing

Gathering fills the shelf; installing is the other half, and the only thing in
Mindweaver that writes into a mind project. A skill is copied wherever the
project's agents read it ([D-07](#d-07-one-copy-per-agent-folder)): one copy
in each of its targets (`install::targets`), the folders the target table
sends its agents to (`MindProject::targets`), so a project naming all three
gets a copy in `.claude/skills` for Claude and one in `.agents/skills` that
Codex and OpenCode share, and one whose settings name `targets` a copy in
each folder they name, for all of them ([a project's own
targets](#a-projects-own-targets)). A project a `mind.toml` marks names no
agents, and gets one copy in the folder its marker names, as before. A rule is
no folder, and reaches a project's agents otherwise: through the block of its
`AGENTS.md` and Claude's files, rendered with every other rule it has
([installing rules](#installing-rules)). Nor is an MCP server, whose payload
is an entry: one in the config file of each agent the project names, by the
fingerprint of what was written there ([installing an MCP
server](#installing-an-mcp-server)).

Not the folder a project's settings say it authors in
([D-06](#d-06-projects-keep-authoring-beside-the-code)): what the workspace
offers goes where the agents read, what the project writes itself stays where
it writes it, and neither is mistaken for the other. Two targets that are one
folder on disk, `.claude/skills` linked to `.agents/skills`, are one target
under the first spelling, as discovery reads them once; two copies put in
place in one folder would find each other there.

### The folder is named twice, on purpose

Gathering keeps the folder name the **source** used. Installing files the copy
under the name the skill **declares**. That looks inconsistent and is not.

On the shelf, renaming would repair a symptom and hide it: a skill whose
directory disagrees with its front matter is something `validate` exists to
report, and the shelf is a record of what a source actually contained. Inside a
project the same mismatch is not a report, it is a skill that lists fine and
never loads: the directory name is how an agent finds what it was told to
invoke. So the copy is filed under the declared name, and the disagreement
stays where it belongs, upstream.

### Held to the rules on the way in

What gathering took leniently, installing takes strictly: a skill whose name
or description breaks the rules is offered, so nothing gathered is hidden, and
refused, so nothing an agent would skip lands in a project. The check reads the
files about to be copied rather than what the ledger noted when they were
gathered, because the shelf is a folder anybody can edit and the workspace's own
are edited as a matter of course. For the same reason it compares what they
declare with the folder the copy is about to be filed in, the name the ledger
recorded: a shelf copy edited to declare another name, or a skill its source
renamed while the record of its old name stayed, would otherwise land under one
name declaring another. A refused skill is fixed upstream and gathered again,
or, if it is the workspace's own, fixed where it is.

### It only manages what it installed

The ledger records every installation against `(project, kind, name)`, with
each copy it wrote as a target of it (its path, and the one agent it is for,
or none for `.agents/skills`, which two agents share), and that record is what
separates a file this tool put there from one somebody wrote. Standing is
worked out over every target, by the path each record names rather than by
its name (`Ledger::copies`, as a listing marks installed copies): a skill
present anywhere it would be written, and unrecorded there, is
`Standing::Foreign`, whatever the other targets hold. Foreign is inert in both
directions: never overwritten, never deleted, and the caller is told so,
with the path, rather than obeyed quietly. It becomes Mindweaver's only when
somebody adopts it by name ([adopting what a project already
keeps](#adopting-what-a-project-already-keeps)), as it is. So somebody's skill in
`.claude/skills` refuses the whole install, and `.agents/skills` is not
written either: a copy beside it would hand OpenCode, which reads both, two
different skills of one name. Only the targets refuse, as D-07 has it, not
every folder an agent reads (`Agent::reads`): a project that names OpenCode
and not Claude is sent nothing in `.claude/skills` or `.opencode/skills`,
though OpenCode loads what is there, so somebody's `ship` in one of them does
not stop `.agents/skills/ship` from being written, and OpenCode is then
handed two versions of one skill, which nothing says ([an open
question](#open-questions)). A name installed into one folder does not claim
what somebody keeps under it in another, as when a project names an agent
after the install. Where every copy there is recorded, what each copy the
record names holds says how the installation stands ([an edited copy is
left alone](#an-edited-copy-is-left-alone)): one gone since is
`Standing::Missing`, and the next install puts it back. A listing says the
same of a copy in a project's agents' folders
(`Provenance::Foreign`), and no change to the project's own reaches one
([read where its agents
read](#a-project-marked-by-its-settings-is-read-where-its-agents-read)).

Uninstalling goes by the record, not by where the project would install now:
every copy it names is removed, and nothing else, so a folder of that name in
a target the record does not name stays somebody's. A route the record holds
is followed only when it is a folder of the project named after the skill
(`InstallError::Recorded` otherwise): before records had targets, a removal
was only ever the name joined onto a folder of the project's, and the ledger,
though the workspace's own, is not a reason to delete anywhere else.

Without that, an install screen is a thing that can delete a colleague's work
because a checkbox looked untidy. The rule costs one query and removes the
whole class.

The record names the project by its route from the workspace, taken to where
the workspace's own entry for it leads (`WeaverWorkspace::spelling_of`)
rather than to however the command spelled the project. `mind` spells its
project the way the operating system reports the directory it runs in,
through no symlink, while a workspace named with `-W` or activated keeps the
spelling it was given. The route between those two is not the entry's, so a
record written under it would be one `mindweaver -p` never finds: a copy nobody
may update, or, the other way round, a record that outlives its copy. A
spelling that already matches the entry as written is kept, so no record
written before is named differently now.

A project has one directory per artifact name in each target, so two shelf
entries offering `commit-style` cannot both be installed. The screen settles
it by unticking the other rather than letting both apply and the second win: a
conflict resolved where somebody can see it happening. A plan handed both
says so rather than choosing ([a batch is planned in
core](#a-batch-is-planned-in-core)).

### An edited copy is left alone

The record keeps a hash of what was written in each copy
([D-04](#d-04-an-edited-copy-is-detected-not-disowned)): once for a skill's
installation, since every copy is staged from one tree, and once a target
for a rule's section and its file, which hold different bytes. That hash,
and what the place the record says it came from offers now
(`install::offered_for`), tell five standings of an installation apart, as
`install::standings` says of each installation and `survey` of each offer of
its name:

- **Current**: every copy holds what was written, and the offer holds it
  still.
- **Outdated**: every copy holds what was written, and the offer has moved
  on. An update brings it up to date, as an install of it does ([bringing
  what was installed up to date](#bringing-what-was-installed-up-to-date)).
- **Edited**: a copy holds anything else: a hand edit, `mind edit`, a
  skill's rename, which rewrites its `name` line, a file added, or a link
  where a file was, which the hash refuses and no install writes. A rule's
  rename moves its file as it is, and is no edit: the copy holds what was
  installed, orphaned while nothing offers it by its new route.
- **Missing**: a copy the record names is not where it was put, and an
  update puts it back, as an install of it does. Every copy gone is still missing rather than absent:
  the ledger records it, and `mindweaver uninstall` forgets it. The install
  screen opens its box empty all the same (`Standing::present`), saying a
  copy is gone, so marking it puts every copy back, as it did when every
  copy gone read as absent: a `git clean -dX` takes every copy of a local
  project at once (and its `.mind` with them, an open question). Held, the
  box could only be marked to be taken out, so one with a copy left is
